title: Choosing the Method
bigQuestion: How does a cook look at a piece of food and know whether it needs ten minutes of high heat or three hours of low?

story.title: The Four-Dollar Roast
story.kicker: Amara's grandmother bought the cheapest beef in the case and served the most tender dinner of the month. The secret was a lid and an afternoon.
paragraphs: Amara went grocery shopping with her grandmother on a Saturday morning, and they stopped at the meat counter. Amara pointed at the ribeye steaks, marbled and bright red, at a price that made her grandmother laugh. "Those are for a birthday," she said. She reached instead for a chuck roast the size of a small brick, wrapped tight in plastic, marked at about a third of the price per pound (example prices). "This one is for a Saturday."

At home, Amara looked at the roast doubtfully. It was tough-looking, with white lines of gristle running through it. Her grandmother patted it dry with a paper towel, salted it all over, and heated 2 Tbsp of oil in a heavy pot until it shimmered. The roast went in with a hiss and she left it alone, four minutes a side, until every face was dark brown. "Do not rush this part," she said. "The color is the flavor."

Out came the roast. In went an onion, two carrots and two celery stalks, chopped rough, and they cooked in the drippings until soft. She poured in two cups of broth and scraped the bottom of the pot with a wooden spoon until all the brown bits let go. The roast went back in, the liquid came halfway up its sides, the lid went on, and the whole pot went into a 325 °F oven. "Now we wait. Three hours, maybe a little more."

Amara checked at the one-hour mark with a fork. The meat was tight and springy and the fork barely went in. At two hours it was softer at the edges. At three hours the fork slid in and the meat pulled apart into strands, the gristle had melted into the sauce, and the kitchen smelled like Sunday. Her grandmother set the pot on the table with rice.

"The steak would have been ruined cooked this way," her grandmother said. "And this roast would have been shoe leather cooked like a steak. It is not about cheap or expensive. It is about knowing what a cut needs." Amara wrote it on the inside cover of her notebook: tender cuts, fast and hot; tough cuts, slow and wet.
story.think: Why would the ribeye have been ruined by three hours in a covered pot, and why would the chuck roast have been ruined by four minutes a side in a hot pan?

lessons.title: Tender Cuts and Tough Cuts
lessons.mainIdea: Muscles that worked hard are tough and need slow moist heat; muscles that did little are tender and need fast dry heat.
reading: Meat is muscle, and muscles that did a lot of work are different from muscles that did not. The shoulder, the leg and the neck of a cow or pig carried the animal's weight all day. Those cuts, such as chuck, brisket, shank and pork shoulder, are full of *connective tissue*, the tough web that holds muscle bundles together, and they are chewy if cooked fast. The muscles along the back did very little, so cuts from there, such as tenderloin, loin chops, ribeye and strip steak, are tender from the start and cost more.

The rule follows from that. *Tender cuts* suit *dry-heat* methods that are fast and hot: grilling, broiling, sautéing, pan-frying, roasting. Cook them just until done and stop; more time only dries them out. *Tough cuts* suit *moist-heat* and combination methods that are slow and gentle: braising, stewing, simmering. Time and moisture turn connective tissue into soft gelatin, and the meat becomes tender and the sauce becomes rich.

The same idea works for poultry, fish and vegetables. Chicken breast is lean and tender, so it dries out with long cooking; sear or roast it just to 165 °F. Chicken thighs and legs have more connective tissue and stay juicy through a braise. Most fish is delicate and cooks in minutes by any method. Hard root vegetables, such as beets and potatoes, need time to soften; tender ones, such as spinach and asparagus, need seconds. Dried beans and whole grains need long simmering to take in water.

Getting this wrong wastes money in both directions. A ribeye braised for three hours turns gray and dry, because it had no connective tissue to melt, only muscle fibers to tighten. A chuck roast grilled for eight minutes is a workout to chew. Learn a few cuts from each group, and you can walk up to any meat counter, buy what is on sale, and know what to do with it.

words.d: meat from a muscle that did little work, such as loin or tenderloin; best cooked fast with dry heat
meat from a hard-working muscle, such as chuck or shank; best cooked slowly with moist heat
the tough web that holds muscle together; it melts into gelatin only with long, gentle, moist cooking
cooking with hot air, hot metal or hot fat and no added liquid: roasting, grilling, sautéing
cooking in or over liquid: simmering, poaching, steaming, braising, stewing

look.title: Sort the Meat Counter
look.text: Eight packages sit in the case: beef chuck roast, pork tenderloin, chicken thighs, beef shank, salmon fillet, boneless chicken breast, pork shoulder, and strip steak. Two friends have a grill and a Dutch oven between them. One wants dinner in 20 minutes; the other is cooking for tomorrow and has all afternoon.
look.prompt: Divide the packages between the two cooks and name the method each will use. Which package could go either way?

check.q: Which cut is the best choice for a fast grill on a weeknight?
choices: Beef shank
Pork shoulder
Pork tenderloin
Beef brisket
check.why: Tenderloin is a little-worked, tender muscle. Shank, shoulder and brisket are tough and need slow moist heat.

check.q: Why does a chuck roast become chewy when it is grilled quickly?
choices: Grilling adds water to the meat
Its connective tissue never has time to turn into gelatin
It has too little fat
Grills are not hot enough for beef
check.why: Connective tissue needs hours of gentle moist heat. A fast sear leaves it tough.

check.q: Which statement about chicken is correct?
choices: Breast meat stays juicy through a long braise
Thighs dry out faster than breasts
Both breasts and thighs are safe at 145 °F
Thighs have more connective tissue and hold up to braising better than breasts
check.why: Thighs are working muscles with more connective tissue. Both cuts of poultry are safe at 165 °F.

lessons.title: Reading the Cut at the Counter
lessons.mainIdea: The label and the look of a cut tell you what it is and how to cook it, and a tough cut on sale is a bargain only if you cook it the slow way.
reading: Stand at the meat counter and read a label. It names the animal, the primal, which is the large section of the animal the cut came from, and the cut itself: beef chuck shoulder roast, pork loin chops, chicken thighs bone-in. It also shows the weight, the price per pound, and the total price, and a sell-by date. The price per pound is the number to compare; a big package with a low total may still cost more per pound than a smaller one (example: 2.5 lb at $4.00 per lb is $10.00; 1.5 lb at $6.00 per lb is $9.00, but the first is the better unit price).

Now look at the meat. Thin white lines of fat running through the muscle are *marbling*, and marbling means tenderness and flavor in a cut cooked with dry heat. Thick white bands and silvery sheets are connective tissue; they mean the cut wants a braise. Bone-in cuts cook more slowly than boneless but stay moister. A cut labeled ground has been chopped fine and must be cooked to 160 °F, whatever the animal, because any bacteria on the surface got mixed all the way through.

The word roast on a label is a shape, not a method. A chuck roast is tough and needs braising; a rib roast is tender and is roasted with dry heat. The word steak means a slice; a strip steak is tender and a round steak is tough. When in doubt, the primal tells you: chuck, brisket, round, shank and shoulder are working muscles, and rib, loin and tenderloin are not. A quick search on the primal name settles most questions.

Buy safely and get it home cold. Choose packages that are cold to the touch, tightly sealed and not leaking. Pick up meat last and bag it separately from produce so juices cannot drip onto food that will be eaten raw. Refrigerate it at 40 °F or below within two hours, one hour if it is over 90 °F outside, and store it on the bottom shelf in a tray so nothing below it can be dripped on.

words.d: one of the large sections an animal is first divided into, such as chuck, rib, loin or round
thin streaks of fat inside the muscle that make a cut tender and flavorful with dry heat
the unit price on a meat label; the number to compare between packages
the date the store must sell the package by; cook or freeze it within a day or two after

look.title: Two Packages of Beef (Example Prices)
rows: chuck roast, 3.0 lb, price per lb
ribeye steaks, 1.5 lb, price per lb
look.cite: Example figures for practice, not current store prices
look.prompt: Work out the cost per serving of each package. Which one is the budget choice, and what method does it require?

check.q: A label reads beef round steak, on sale. What does the primal name tell you about cooking it?
choices: It is tender and should be grilled fast
It is from a working muscle and suits slow moist heat
It must be cooked to 160 °F because it is ground
It cannot be frozen
check.why: Round is the hind leg, a working muscle. Round steak is lean and tough and does best braised or simmered.

check.q: Why must ground beef reach 160 °F when a whole steak is safe at 145 °F with a rest?
choices: Ground beef is fattier
Ground beef is usually thicker
Grinding mixes surface bacteria all the way through the meat
Ground beef is older when sold
check.why: On a whole cut, bacteria are only on the surface, which sears. Grinding spreads them throughout, so the center must reach 160 °F.

check.q: Where should raw meat be stored in the refrigerator?
choices: On the bottom shelf in a tray so it cannot drip onto other food
On the top shelf so it stays coldest
In the door where it is easy to reach
Next to the salad greens
check.why: Raw meat juices carry bacteria. The bottom shelf keeps drips off food that will be eaten without cooking.

lessons.title: Oven Temperatures and What They Do
lessons.mainIdea: A low oven cooks gently and evenly, a moderate oven cooks most things, and a hot oven browns and crisps, so the temperature you choose is a choice about what the surface and center should look like.
reading: Ovens have a dial from about 200 to 500 °F, and cooks group the range into bands. *Low*, about 250 to 325 °F, is for long, gentle cooking: braises, slow-roasted tough cuts, custards, meringues, and holding food warm. Heat creeps in slowly, so the outside of the food is not much more cooked than the center by the time it is done. A *moderate* oven, 350 to 375 °F, is the everyday setting for cakes, cookies, casseroles, meatloaf and chicken pieces. It is hot enough to brown the surface over the course of the cooking but slow enough for the center to catch up.

A *hot* oven, 400 to 450 °F, is for roasting vegetables, roasting a chicken with crisp skin, baking bread, and anything that should have dark edges and a crisp outside. Heat hits the surface fast and drives the Maillard reaction. A *very hot* oven, 475 to 500 °F, is for pizza, flatbread and searing a roast before turning the oven down. At these settings, minutes matter, and food that is thin or sugary can burn while you turn your back.

Thickness decides how the bands play out. A thin sheet of cookies at 375 °F browns and sets in about 10 minutes. A thick loaf of meatloaf at the same temperature needs an hour, because heat must travel to the center by conduction. A large roast at 450 °F would be black outside before the center was safe, which is why big things go in cooler ovens for longer, or start hot and finish low. When you change a recipe's pan size or piece size, expect to change the time and maybe the temperature too.

Two habits make ovens honest. First, an oven thermometer, because many home ovens run 25 °F or more off the dial. Second, the middle rack unless the recipe says otherwise; the top rack is closer to the broiler element and browns faster, and the bottom rack sits near the heating element and burns bottoms. Keep the door closed; every peek costs heat and time.

words.d: about 250 to 325 °F; gentle, even cooking for braises, custards and slow roasts
350 to 375 °F; the everyday setting for cakes, cookies and casseroles
400 to 450 °F; roasting vegetables, crisp-skinned chicken and bread with dark edges
475 to 500 °F; pizza, flatbread and a fast sear before turning the oven down

look.title: Oven Bands and Typical Uses
look.cite: Common cookbook oven bands; exact settings vary by recipe
look.prompt: A recipe says to bake a custard at 425 °F. What band is that, and why is it probably a misprint?

check.q: Which oven setting is right for roasting vegetables with dark, crisp edges?
check.why: A hot oven drives browning fast. Lower settings soften vegetables without crisping them.

check.q: A cook puts a large beef roast in a 475 °F oven for the whole cooking time. What is the likely result?
choices: Perfectly even doneness
A burnt outside before the center is safe
A pale, unbrowned surface
The roast finishes faster and just as well
check.why: Heat must travel to the center by conduction. A very hot oven chars the outside long before a thick center is done.

check.q: Why do cooks hang an oven thermometer inside the oven?
choices: Many ovens run 25 °F or more off the dial
It speeds up preheating
It keeps the oven from overheating
Recipes require it
check.why: The dial is a setting, not a measurement. A thermometer shows the real temperature so recipes work as written.

lessons.title: Braising a Tough Cut
lessons.mainIdea: A braise is brown, soften, deglaze, submerge halfway, cover, and simmer low for hours, and each step is there for a reason.
reading: Here is a full braise for a 3-pound beef chuck roast, feeding six to eight. Take the roast out of the package, pat it dry all over with paper towels, and season it with about 1 tsp of salt and some black pepper. Set a heavy lidded pot, such as a Dutch oven, over medium-high heat and add 2 Tbsp of oil. When the oil shimmers, lower the roast in away from you. Leave it alone 3 to 4 minutes, then turn it with tongs and brown every side. Do not rush; deep brown is the goal.

Move the roast to a plate. Add 1 chopped onion, 2 chopped carrots and 2 chopped celery stalks to the pot and cook, stirring, until soft and lightly browned, about 6 to 8 minutes. Add 2 cloves of chopped garlic for the last minute. Pour in 2 cups of broth and scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon until every brown bit lifts off; this is *deglazing*, and those bits carry most of the flavor. Return the roast and any juices from the plate. The liquid should come about halfway up the meat, so add a little more if needed.

Bring the liquid to a simmer, put on the lid, and move the pot to a 325 °F oven. The oven surrounds the pot with steady heat from all sides, which is easier than a stovetop burner that can scorch the bottom. Check once an hour: the liquid should show a few lazy bubbles, and if it is boiling hard, lower the oven 25 °F. At about 2 1/2 hours, test with a fork. When it slides in and twists the meat apart with no fight, it is done, usually 3 to 3 1/2 hours.

Move the meat to a board, tent it with foil, and let it rest 15 minutes. Skim the fat off the liquid with a spoon, or pour it into a measuring cup and let the fat rise, then spoon it off. Simmer the liquid a few minutes to thicken it, taste, and add salt if needed. Slice or shred the meat and serve it with the sauce. Cool leftovers within two hours and refrigerate; reheat to 165 °F. A braise is one of the most forgiving dishes there is, as long as it never boils and never runs dry.

words.d: a heavy pot with a tight lid that can go from stovetop to oven; the standard braising pot
to pour liquid into a hot pan and scrape up the browned bits stuck to the bottom
to lay a loose sheet of foil over cooked meat while it rests, so it stays warm without steaming
to spoon the fat or foam off the surface of a liquid

look.title: Where Did the Braise Go Wrong?
look.text: A student braises a chuck roast. He browns it well, adds the vegetables, pours in the broth without scraping the pot, fills the pot until the roast is fully covered, leaves the lid off, and sets the oven to 400 °F. After two hours the liquid has boiled down to a half inch, the top of the roast is dry and dark, and the bottom half is tough. The bits on the bottom of the pot are black.
look.prompt: Find four mistakes and explain what each one did to the roast.

check.q: What is deglazing and why is it done?
choices: Adding liquid and scraping up the browned bits so their flavor goes into the sauce
Pouring off the fat before adding vegetables
Rinsing the pot between browning and simmering
Covering the meat completely with liquid
check.why: The fond on the pot bottom is concentrated flavor. Liquid and scraping lift it into the braise.

check.q: How high should the liquid come in a braise?
choices: Barely covering the bottom of the pot
About halfway up the meat
Completely covering the meat by an inch
Just enough to steam it
check.why: A braise is partly submerged. The bottom simmers and the top steams under the lid, giving both tenderness and flavor.

check.q: Why move a braise from the stovetop into a 325 °F oven?
choices: The oven cooks it faster
The oven browns the top of the meat
The oven browns the vegetables
The oven heats the pot evenly from all sides so the bottom does not scorch
check.why: A burner heats only the pot bottom. Oven heat surrounds the pot and keeps a steady, gentle simmer.

lessons.title: Stir-Frying
lessons.mainIdea: Stir-frying is a very hot pan, everything cut and ready before the heat goes on, and ingredients added in order from slowest-cooking to fastest.
reading: A stir-fry takes five minutes to cook and twenty to prepare, and the preparation is the technique. Because the pan is so hot, there is no time to chop while cooking. Cut everything first and line it up in bowls in the order it will go in. For a chicken and vegetable stir-fry for four: 1 pound boneless chicken thighs sliced thin across the grain; 1 sliced onion; 2 cups broccoli florets; 1 sliced bell pepper; 2 cloves minced garlic and 1 Tbsp minced ginger; and a sauce of 3 Tbsp soy sauce, 1 Tbsp water and 1 tsp cornstarch stirred together.

Set a wok or a large heavy skillet over the highest heat and let it get very hot, a full two minutes, until a drop of water skitters and vanishes. Add 1 Tbsp of a high-heat oil such as canola and swirl. Add the chicken in a single layer, let it sit 30 seconds to brown, then toss and stir until it is no longer pink, about 3 minutes. Move it to a clean plate. This is cooking in batches: the protein first, alone, so the pan stays hot.

Add another tablespoon of oil. Add the onion and broccoli, the slowest vegetables, and stir-fry 2 minutes; splash in 2 Tbsp of water and cover for a minute if the broccoli needs help. Add the pepper and cook 1 minute. Push the vegetables to the sides, drop the garlic and ginger in the middle for 30 seconds until fragrant, then stir everything together. Return the chicken, pour in the sauce, and toss for about a minute until the sauce thickens and coats everything. Serve at once over rice.

The failures all trace to heat. A pan that is not hot enough steams the vegetables gray. Too much food at once drops the temperature. Wet vegetables straight from rinsing do the same, so dry them. Thick, uneven pieces cook unevenly, so cut thin and cut alike. Keep the food moving so nothing burns, keep a lid handy in case oil flares, and keep your sleeves and towels away from the burner.

words.d: to cook small, even pieces very fast in a little oil over the highest heat, stirring constantly
a wide, deep, round-bottomed pan made for stir-frying
slicing meat crosswise to the lines of muscle fiber, which makes each bite more tender
garlic, ginger, onion and similar ingredients added for flavor and fragrance

look.title: Order the Wok
look.text: The ingredients for a stir-fry are ready: sliced chicken, broccoli florets, sliced onion, sliced bell pepper, minced garlic and ginger, and a soy-cornstarch sauce. Here are the steps, scrambled: add the sauce and toss until it thickens; cook the chicken alone and set it aside; heat the pan until a drop of water skitters; add garlic and ginger for 30 seconds; add onion and broccoli; add the pepper; return the chicken.
look.prompt: Put the steps in order and explain why the chicken goes in first and alone, and why the garlic goes in so late.

check.q: Why does a stir-fry cook the protein first, alone, and then set it aside?
choices: So the vegetables absorb the meat flavor
So the pan stays hot and the meat browns instead of steaming
Because meat takes longer than vegetables to cut
So the sauce can be added earlier
check.why: Everything at once crowds the pan and drops the temperature. Batches keep the heat high.

check.q: Why are garlic and ginger added near the end rather than at the start?
choices: They need the least heat to release flavor and burn quickly over high heat
They cook slowly and need to sit on the sauce
They add water to the pan
They must touch the chicken
check.why: Minced aromatics burn in seconds on high heat. Thirty seconds at the end makes them fragrant, not bitter.

check.q: A stir-fry comes out with gray, limp vegetables sitting in liquid. Which is the most likely cause?
choices: Too much garlic
The chicken was sliced across the grain
The pan was not hot enough or was overloaded
The sauce had cornstarch in it
check.why: Low heat or too much food means the vegetables steam in their own water instead of searing.

lessons.title: Making a Pan Sauce
lessons.mainIdea: A pan sauce turns the browned bits left after searing into a sauce in about three minutes: pour off fat, deglaze, reduce, and finish with butter off the heat.
reading: You have just seared two pork chops and moved them to a plate to rest. Look at the pan: the bottom is dotted with dark brown, sticky bits, the *fond*, and it is the best flavor in the kitchen. Do not wash it. A pan sauce takes about three minutes and uses what is already there. It works for chops, chicken breasts, steaks and fish, and it is the fastest way to make a plain weeknight dinner taste like more.

Pour off all but about 1 Tbsp of the fat, keeping the fond. Set the pan over medium heat and add 1 Tbsp of finely chopped shallot or onion; cook it 30 seconds until soft. Pour in 1/2 cup of liquid: chicken broth, or half broth and half apple juice, or broth with a splash of vinegar. Pour it in away from you, because it will sputter. Scrape the bottom with a wooden spoon as it bubbles until every bit of fond has dissolved into the liquid. That is deglazing, the same move as in a braise, just faster.

Now *reduce*: let the liquid boil until about half of it has cooked off, 1 to 2 minutes, and it looks slightly thicker and coats the spoon. Reducing concentrates flavor because the water leaves and the flavor stays. Add any juices that have collected on the plate under the resting meat. Take the pan off the heat and swirl in 1 Tbsp of cold butter, cut in pieces, until it melts into a glossy sauce. This is *mounting* with butter; do it off the heat, because boiling the butter breaks the sauce and makes it greasy.

Taste, add a pinch of salt or a squeeze of lemon, and spoon it over the meat. The mistakes are few and clear. Black fond means the sear went too far, and the sauce will be bitter; wipe the pan and skip the sauce. Too much fat left in the pan makes a slick, greasy sauce. Skipping the reduction gives a thin, watery one. And adding the butter over a hot burner makes it separate. Three minutes, four steps, and a plain chop becomes dinner.

words.d: the browned bits stuck to the pan after searing meat; the flavor base of a pan sauce
to boil a liquid so water evaporates, making it thicker and more concentrated in flavor
to swirl cold butter into a sauce off the heat so it turns glossy and slightly thick
a small, mild member of the onion family often used in sauces

look.title: A Sauce in Four Lines
look.text: Line 1: pour off fat, leave 1 Tbsp and all the fond. Line 2: add shallot, then 1/2 cup broth; scrape the bottom clean. Line 3: boil until half is gone and it coats a spoon. Line 4: off the heat, swirl in 1 Tbsp cold butter; taste; spoon over the meat. A student did all four but added the butter while the burner was still on high, and the sauce turned into a greasy puddle with butter floating on top.
look.prompt: Explain what happened at line 4 and how the student could have saved the sauce.

check.q: What does reducing a sauce do?
choices: Cools it down before serving
Adds fat so it is richer
Cooks off water so the flavor is stronger and the sauce is thicker
Makes it safe to eat
check.why: Boiling drives off water. The flavor compounds stay, so a reduced sauce is more concentrated and thicker.

check.q: Why is the butter added off the heat?
choices: Butter must be cold to taste right
Boiling butter breaks the sauce and makes it greasy
The pan is too hot to touch
Butter does not melt over a burner
check.why: Mounting with butter works only when the sauce is hot but not boiling. Boiling separates the butter fat out.

check.q: The fond in the pan has turned black. What should the cook do?
choices: Add more broth to dilute the bitterness
Add sugar to balance it
Reduce it longer
Wipe the pan and skip the sauce, since burnt fond makes a bitter sauce
check.why: Burnt fond is char, not flavor. No amount of liquid or reduction removes the bitterness.

lessons.title: The Thermometer Decides
lessons.mainIdea: Color, time and touch are guesses; a food thermometer in the thickest part, away from bone, is the only way to know meat is safe and not overcooked.
reading: A chicken thigh can look done on the outside and be pink at the bone. A burger can be brown all the way through and still be under 160 °F, or gray and dry at 180 °F. Cooking times in recipes are averages for a certain thickness in a certain oven. The only measurement that tells you both safety and doneness is the internal temperature, and the tool is an instant-read *food thermometer*, which costs about as much as a pound of steak and lasts for years.

To use it, push the probe into the thickest part of the food, away from bone, fat and the pan, since bone and metal read hot. Go in from the side for thin pieces such as chops and burgers so the tip sits in the center. Wait for the reading to settle, a few seconds on a digital model. Check more than one spot on a large roast. Wash the probe with hot soapy water between checks on raw and cooked food, and after every use.

The USDA safe minimums are the numbers to memorize. Poultry, whole or pieces or ground: 165 °F. Ground meats, beef, pork and lamb: 160 °F. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb and veal, such as steaks, chops and roasts: 145 °F, then rest 3 minutes before cutting. Fish: 145 °F, or until it flakes. Egg dishes: cooked until firm. Leftovers and casseroles reheated: 165 °F. Those temperatures kill the bacteria that cause food poisoning; below them, you are guessing.

A thermometer also saves food from overcooking. Meat keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, a few degrees for a chop and 5 to 10 for a large roast, so many cooks pull a roast a few degrees under the target and let the rest finish it. Test the thermometer's accuracy now and then: in a glass of ice water with a little liquid, it should read 32 °F. If it does not, adjust it or replace it.

words.d: an instant-read probe that shows the internal temperature of food in seconds
where the probe goes: the center of the largest part of the food, away from bone and pan
the USDA temperature at which the bacteria that cause illness are killed
checking a thermometer in ice water, where it should read 32 °F

look.title: USDA Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures
rows: beef, pork, lamb, veal whole cuts, then rest 3 min
look.cite: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
look.prompt: A bone-in chicken thigh reads 165 °F next to the bone and 150 °F in the meat an inch away. Is it done? Where should the probe have gone?

check.q: Where should the thermometer probe go in a bone-in pork chop?
choices: Touching the bone, since that is the hottest part
Into the thickest part of the meat, away from the bone, from the side
Just under the surface
Into the pan drippings
check.why: Bone conducts heat and reads high. The center of the thickest meat is the last place to reach temperature.

check.q: A turkey burger reads 158 °F. Is it safe to serve?
choices: Yes, all burgers are safe at 155 °F
Yes, turkey is safe at 145 °F
No, ground poultry must reach 165 °F
No, all ground meat must reach 175 °F
check.why: Ground poultry follows the poultry rule: 165 °F. Ground beef, pork and lamb need 160 °F.

check.q: How do you check that a food thermometer is reading correctly?
choices: Put it in ice water; it should read 32 °F
Put it in the oven; it should match the dial
Hold it in the air; it should read 70 °F
Compare it to the microwave clock
check.why: Ice water is a fixed 32 °F. A thermometer that reads off in ice water will read off in a roast.

lessons.title: Resting Meat
lessons.mainIdea: Meat rests for a few minutes after cooking so the temperature finishes rising and the juices settle, and cutting too soon leaves those juices on the board.
reading: Slice a steak the second it comes off the grill and watch the board: a puddle of juice runs out, and the slices go dry and gray at the edges. Slice one that has rested 5 minutes and the juice stays in the meat. *Resting* means moving cooked meat to a plate or board, tenting it loosely with foil, and waiting before cutting. During cooking, the outside of the meat is hotter and tighter than the center, and the juices get pushed toward the middle. Resting lets the heat even out and the fibers relax so the juices redistribute.

Resting also finishes the cooking. The hot outer layers keep passing heat inward after the meat leaves the pan, so the center temperature keeps climbing. This *carryover cooking* is about 3 to 5 °F for a chop or steak and 5 to 10 °F for a large roast. That is why the USDA includes a 3-minute rest in the 145 °F rule for whole cuts: the meat reaches and holds its safe temperature during the rest. Cooks aiming for a certain doneness pull the meat a few degrees early and let carryover land it.

How long to rest depends on size. A chop, a chicken thigh or a small steak: 3 to 5 minutes. A whole chicken: 10 to 15 minutes. A large roast or a turkey: 15 to 30 minutes. Tent, do not wrap; a tight wrap traps steam and turns a crisp crust soft. The meat will stay hot longer than you expect. Use the time to make the pan sauce or finish the vegetables.

Two cautions. Resting is for the finishing of cooked meat; it does not replace reaching a safe temperature, and it is not a rest on the counter for an hour. Cooked food should be served or refrigerated within two hours. And resting applies to meat, not to vegetables, pasta or fish, which are best served at once. Fish in particular goes from flaky to dry in a few minutes of waiting.

words.d: letting cooked meat sit a few minutes before cutting so the juices settle and the temperature evens out
the rise in internal temperature after meat leaves the heat, a few degrees for a chop and up to 10 for a roast
to spread back out; the juices move from the center back through the whole piece as it rests

look.title: The Board Tells the Story
look.text: Two identical strip steaks come off the grill at 140 °F. Steak A is sliced right away. Steak B sits tented on a board for 5 minutes; when a thermometer goes in before slicing it reads 145 °F. Steak A's board is flooded with red juice and the slices look dry. Steak B's board has a teaspoon of juice and the slices are pink and moist from edge to edge.
look.prompt: Explain both the temperature rise in Steak B and the puddle under Steak A. Which steak met the USDA rule for whole cuts?

check.q: What is carryover cooking?
choices: Reheating leftovers the next day
Cooking a second batch in the same pan
The internal temperature continuing to rise after meat leaves the heat
Cooking meat in its own juices
check.why: The hot outer layers keep passing heat inward. A roast can climb 5 to 10 °F while it rests.

check.q: Why tent resting meat loosely with foil instead of wrapping it tightly?
choices: A tight wrap traps steam and softens the crust
Foil cools the meat faster
Tight foil stops carryover cooking
Tenting makes the meat safe to eat
check.why: Steam trapped under a tight wrap turns a crisp, browned surface soggy. A loose tent keeps warmth without steaming.

check.q: Which food should NOT be rested before serving?
choices: A whole roast chicken
A beef roast
A pork chop
A fish fillet
check.why: Fish is delicate and dries out quickly. Serve it as soon as it flakes; rest only meat and poultry.

lessons.title: Cooking Rice and Other Grains
lessons.mainIdea: Grains cook by soaking up a measured amount of simmering water under a lid, so the ratio, the low heat and the closed lid matter more than anything else.
reading: Rice is the side dish half the world eats every day, and the method is simple if the ratio is right. For long-grain white rice: measure 1 cup of rice into a fine strainer and rinse it under cold water until the water runs mostly clear, which washes off surface starch that would make it gummy. Put it in a pot with 2 cups of water and 1/2 tsp of salt. Bring to a boil over high heat, stir once, then turn the heat to the lowest setting, cover tightly, and simmer 18 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let it stand, still covered, 5 to 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork.

The lid is the whole trick. The rice is not boiling in a big pot of water; it is absorbing a measured amount of water and steam. Lift the lid and steam escapes, the water runs short, and the bottom scorches while the top is crunchy. Stir it during cooking and the grains release starch and clump. If the pot is too thin, the bottom burns at even the lowest heat; a heavy pot or a flame tamer fixes that. Rice on the bottom that is stuck but not burnt is called the crust and some cooks fight over it.

Other grains follow the same pattern with different ratios and times, so a chart is worth keeping. Brown rice: 1 cup rice, 2 1/2 cups water, about 45 minutes, because the bran layer slows the water down. Quinoa: 1 cup, 2 cups water, 15 minutes, rinsed first to remove its bitter coating. Oatmeal from rolled oats: 1 cup oats, 2 cups water, 5 minutes stirred. Pasta and couscous are different: pasta boils in a large pot of salted water and is drained, and couscous is simply soaked in an equal amount of boiling water for 5 minutes.

Cooked rice has one safety rule that surprises people. Rice can carry a bacterium whose spores survive cooking, and if cooked rice sits at room temperature it can produce toxins that reheating will not destroy. So treat rice like any leftover: cool it quickly, refrigerate within two hours at 40 °F or below, use it within a few days, and reheat it to 165 °F. Rice left in the cooker overnight is not a leftover; it is trash.

words.d: cooking a grain in a measured amount of water under a lid until all the water is taken up
to run cold water through rice in a strainer to wash off surface starch
to lift and separate cooked rice gently with a fork so it does not pack down
the outer layer of a whole grain, which makes brown rice chewier and slower to cook

look.title: Grain to Water: Cups of Water per Cup of Grain
look.cite: Common package directions; brands vary slightly
look.prompt: You need 3 cups of dry brown rice for a class. How much water, and how long will it take from boil to fluff?

check.q: A pot of white rice is scorched on the bottom and crunchy on top. What most likely happened?
choices: Too much water was used
The lid was lifted during cooking and steam escaped
The rice was rinsed too well
The salt was left out
check.why: The absorption method depends on trapped steam. Lifting the lid lets water escape, so the pot runs dry before the top cooks.

check.q: How much water for 2 cups of dry long-grain white rice?
choices: 2 cups
3 cups
4 cups
6 cups
check.why: The ratio is 2 cups of water per cup of rice. Two cups of rice needs 4 cups of water.

check.q: Why is cooked rice left out overnight unsafe even after reheating?
choices: It loses its vitamins
Reheating makes rice gummy
Rice dries out and becomes hard
Spores that survive cooking can produce toxins at room temperature that reheating does not destroy
check.why: Cooked rice must be refrigerated within two hours. The toxins that form at room temperature are not removed by heat.

lessons.title: Cooking Dried Beans
lessons.mainIdea: Dried beans need a soak, a long gentle simmer with salt, and, for kidney beans, a hard ten-minute boil first; done right they cost a fraction of canned.
reading: A one-pound bag of dried beans makes about 6 cups cooked, the same as roughly four cans, for a fraction of the price (example: a $1.50 bag against $1.00 or more per can). The trade is time. Pour the beans onto a sheet pan and pick out any stones or shriveled ones, then rinse. *Soak* them in a large bowl covered by three inches of cold water for 8 hours or overnight; they will double in size. Or use the quick soak: cover with water, boil 2 minutes, turn off the heat, and let stand 1 hour. Drain either way.

Put the soaked beans in a pot with fresh water to cover by two inches, add 1 tsp of salt and, if you like, a bay leaf, half an onion or a clove of garlic. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer and partly cover. Skim any foam in the first minutes. Check every 20 minutes and add hot water if the beans show above the surface. Most beans take 1 to 2 hours; older beans take longer. They are done when several beans in a row are creamy all the way through with no chalky center.

One kind of bean has a special rule. Raw or undercooked red kidney beans contain a natural toxin that causes severe stomach illness, and a slow cooker does not get hot enough to destroy it. After soaking, boil kidney beans hard, at a full rolling boil, for at least 10 minutes before you turn them down to simmer. That step, from the FDA's guidance, applies to red kidney beans in particular, and it is a good habit for all dried beans.

Lentils and split peas are the shortcut: no soak, 20 to 30 minutes at a simmer. Beans do not get tender in a hard boil, which bursts the skins, and they cook slowly if the water is very hard or if a lot of acid, such as tomatoes, goes in early; add tomatoes near the end. Cool cooked beans in their liquid within two hours, refrigerate up to about four days, or freeze in 2-cup portions, which is one can's worth, ready for a soup or a pot of chili.

words.d: to cover dried beans with cold water for hours so they take in water and cook evenly
boil beans 2 minutes, turn off the heat and let stand 1 hour instead of soaking overnight
the family of plants that includes beans, lentils, peas and peanuts
the hardest boil, with big bubbles breaking across the whole surface; used for 10 minutes on kidney beans

look.title: Chili in the Slow Cooker
look.text: A student wants to make chili for a class event. She rinses a pound of dried red kidney beans, puts them straight into a slow cooker with a can of tomatoes, onion, spices and water, and sets it to low for 8 hours. At serving time the beans are still firm, and by evening several classmates have bad stomach cramps.
look.prompt: Name three things that went wrong, including the one that made people sick, and write the safe version of her plan.

check.q: What step is required for red kidney beans that many other beans do not strictly need?
choices: Adding baking soda to the water
A full rolling boil for at least 10 minutes before simmering
Cooking them in a slow cooker on low
Cooking without salt
check.why: Raw kidney beans contain a toxin that a slow cooker's heat does not destroy. A 10-minute hard boil does.

check.q: Why should tomatoes be added near the end of cooking a pot of beans?
choices: Tomatoes lose color if cooked long
Tomatoes make the beans foam
Acid slows the beans from getting tender
Tomatoes boil off too much water
check.why: Acidic ingredients firm up bean skins and slow softening. Add them once the beans are already tender.

check.q: About how many cups of cooked beans does a one-pound bag of dried beans make?
choices: About 6 cups, roughly four cans' worth
About 2 cups, one can's worth
About 1 cup
About 12 cups
check.why: Dried beans roughly triple in volume. A pound gives about 6 cups cooked, the same as about four 15-ounce cans.

review.q: Which cut belongs in a three-hour braise rather than on a hot grill?
choices: Ribeye steak
Pork tenderloin
Salmon fillet
Beef chuck roast
review.why: Chuck is a working shoulder muscle full of connective tissue. Only long, moist heat makes it tender.

review.q: In a braise, what does deglazing accomplish?
choices: It removes the fat
It lifts the browned fond into the liquid so its flavor is in the sauce
It cools the pot before the oven
It thickens the sauce with flour
review.why: The fond is concentrated browned flavor stuck to the pot. Liquid and scraping dissolve it into the braise.

review.q: A chicken breast reads 150 °F in the thickest part. What should the cook do?
choices: Serve it; chicken is safe at 145 °F
Rest it 3 minutes and serve
Keep cooking until it reads 165 °F
Slice it to check the color
review.why: All poultry must reach 165 °F. Color is not a reliable test.

review.q: Why does a stir-fry require everything to be cut before the pan is heated?
choices: The pan is so hot that there is no time to chop once cooking starts
Cut vegetables taste better after sitting
The oil must be added last
The sauce thickens while the vegetables wait
review.why: Stir-frying takes minutes over the highest heat. Preparation is the technique.

review.q: Which oven band would you use to bake a pizza?
choices: Low, 300 °F
Moderate, 350 °F
Hot, 425 °F
Very hot, 500 °F
review.why: Pizza needs the hottest home oven so the crust browns and crisps before the topping dries out.

review.q: A roast is pulled from the oven at 140 °F and rests 15 minutes under a foil tent. What happens to its temperature?
choices: It drops at once to room temperature
It rises several degrees from carryover cooking
It stays exactly at 140 °F
It rises to 165 °F
review.why: Heat from the outer layers keeps moving inward. A large roast can climb 5 to 10 °F while it rests.

review.q: Which grain-to-water ratio is right for long-grain white rice by the absorption method?
choices: 1 cup rice to 1 cup water
1 cup rice to 4 cups water
1 cup rice to 2 cups water
1 cup rice to 3 cups water
review.why: White rice takes up two cups of water per cup of rice in about 18 minutes under a lid.

review.q: A student wants to make a pan sauce but the bits in the pan are black. Why does that matter?
choices: Burnt fond makes a bitter sauce, so the pan should be wiped and the sauce skipped
Black fond has the most flavor
Black fond means the meat is undercooked
The sauce will be too thick
review.why: Browning past deep golden is char. No liquid or reduction takes the bitterness out.
